## Intelligent hair removal lasers: artificial intelligence, melanin analysis and treatment safety

HTML source: [Intelligent hair removal lasers: artificial intelligence, melanin analysis and treatment safety](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/blog/artificial-intelligence-in-laser-hair-removal/)

Language: English

Other languages: [Polski](https://ltsmarket.pl/blog/sztuczna-inteligencja-w-epilacji-laserowej/), [Русский](https://ltsmarket.pl/ru/blog/iskusstvennyy-intellekt-v-lazernoy-epilyatsii/)

> Discover how AI, melanin measurements, optical skin analysis and temperature sensors can support safer and more personalised laser hair removal.

LTS Market Blog

24.11.2026 · LTS Market

The future of laser hair removal: technology, effectiveness and safety. Part 2.

For many years, developments in laser hair removal equipment primarily focused on increasing power, improving cooling and introducing additional wavelengths.

Today, another direction is becoming increasingly important. Equipment can do more than generate laser radiation. It can collect information about the skin, monitor its operating parameters and support practitioners in making decisions.

Melanin measurements, spectrophotometry, digital dermoscopy, temperature sensors and image analysis algorithms create new opportunities for treatment personalisation.

Artificial intelligence, or AI, is also appearing increasingly frequently in equipment descriptions.

However, not every automatic function constitutes artificial intelligence. Understanding the differences between measurement, automation and machine learning is essential when evaluating modern equipment.

### Why is skin assessment important?

Laser hair removal is based on selective photothermolysis. Light energy absorbed by melanin within the hair is converted into heat, which affects structures within the hair follicle.

However, melanin is also present in the epidermis.

Some laser energy may be absorbed by the skin before reaching the follicle. The amount absorbed depends on factors including pigmentation, wavelength and pulse characteristics.

Accurate skin assessment is therefore important for both treatment effectiveness and safety.

Practitioners traditionally rely on client interviews, visual assessment and the Fitzpatrick skin phototype classification.

These methods remain necessary but can be supplemented with objective optical measurements.

### The Fitzpatrick scale and actual melanin content

The Fitzpatrick classification includes six skin phototypes. It was originally developed to describe skin responses to sunlight, particularly the tendency to burn or tan.

A phototype is not a direct measurement of melanin concentration.

Two individuals with the same phototype may have different levels of pigmentation. Differences may also exist between anatomical areas of the same individual.

Seasonal changes, recent sun exposure and local pigmentation variations are also relevant.

Consequently, phototype alone may not provide all the information required for treatment parameter selection.

Objective pigmentation measurements can provide an additional source of information.

![Phototype and pigmentation measurement](https://ltsmarket.pl/assets/img/blog/ai-hair-removal/en/phototype-vs-melanin.svg)

Phototype and pigmentation measurement

### What is skin spectrophotometry?

Spectrophotometry is an optical technique used to analyse how materials absorb or reflect light across different spectral ranges.

In skin assessment, optical measurements can provide information associated with melanin, haemoglobin and other tissue properties.

A simplified measurement process involves the following steps:

1. A light source illuminates the measurement area.
2. Some light is absorbed and scattered within the tissue.
3. A detector records light returning from the skin.
4. Software analyses the signal.
5. The result is presented as a pigmentation index or another optical parameter.

Not every colour sensor is a spectrophotometer. Simpler instruments may use a few selected wavelengths, whereas advanced systems analyse broader spectral ranges.

A melanin index should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of the percentage of melanin in the skin.

Results depend on the measurement method, calibration and algorithms used by the instrument.

![Optical skin analysis](https://ltsmarket.pl/assets/img/blog/ai-hair-removal/en/skin-optical-analysis.svg)

Optical skin analysis

### Is there scientific evidence for melanin measurements?

Quantitative assessment of skin pigmentation has been investigated for many years.

In 2009, Verkruysse and colleagues published a study in the Journal of Biomedical Optics investigating optical measurements of light returning from the skin at 390 nm.

The research involved 23 volunteers and measurements at 749 skin sites.

The authors investigated whether optical measurements could support epidermal pigmentation assessment and estimation of tolerance to laser exposure [[1]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19256693/).

In 2016, a publication examined the use of a melanin meter to support parameter selection for intense pulsed light treatments.

Relationships between pigmentation and epidermal tolerance were incorporated into guidance software. The authors also described experience using the device in more than 300 patients [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27050697/).

In 2018, Lloyd, Graves and Ross published research on melanin measurements and epidermal tolerance during treatment using long-pulsed 755 nm alexandrite and 1064 nm Nd:YAG lasers.

Their findings supported quantitative pigmentation assessment as an additional tool for informing parameter selection [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30020097/).

This does not establish a universal algorithm capable of automatically selecting the settings of every laser.

It does, however, demonstrate a scientific rationale for objective pigmentation assessment.

### Analysing skin responses during treatments

Another development involves optical methods for assessing changes in the skin.

In 2019, researchers published a spectroscopic investigation of erythema associated with laser hair removal.

The study involved 19 participants. Skin reflectance spectra were recorded before and after treatment.

The researchers analysed changes associated with the optical characteristics of haemoglobin and the erythema index [[4]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6499568/).

Such methods may support the development of tools for more objective assessment of skin responses.

However, this does not demonstrate that modern lasers can automatically identify every thermal injury or prevent all adverse events.

Measuring an individual parameter and comprehensively assessing treatment safety are different tasks.

### Temperature sensors and intelligent cooling

Temperature is important both to laser hair removal and to equipment operation.

Modern lasers may incorporate several different temperature sensors:

- Diode module temperature sensors.

- Coolant temperature sensors.

- Handpiece contact surface sensors.

- Skin surface temperature sensors, where supported by the device architecture.

Each sensor measures a different part of the system.

The temperature of the sapphire contact window is not equivalent to skin temperature. Skin surface temperature also does not directly establish the temperature inside the hair follicle.

These distinctions matter when evaluating systems marketed as intelligent cooling.

Automatic regulation may involve continuously measuring temperature, comparing it with a target value and controlling cooling components accordingly.

This is known as closed-loop or feedback control.

Artificial intelligence is not necessarily required for such a system to operate effectively.

![Temperature measurement points](https://ltsmarket.pl/assets/img/blog/ai-hair-removal/en/temperature-monitoring.svg)

Temperature measurement points

### Contact and motion sensors

Certain laser and IPL systems incorporate sensors that assess contact between the handpiece and the skin.

Their purpose may include preventing emission when the handpiece is incorrectly positioned.

Motion sensors are another solution that can support practitioners working in dynamic treatment modes.

Depending on the device architecture, a system may monitor movement, identify deviations or assist with treatment coverage.

These features do not automatically eliminate the risk of excessive skin heating.

Motion sensing does not replace an understanding of energy distribution, treatment overlap and tissue responses.

Examples of contact, pigmentation and motion sensors can also be found in technical documentation for IPL devices [[5]](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf23/K231215.pdf).

Such functions should not be automatically attributed to every professional diode laser.

### Dermoscopy and image analysis

Digital dermoscopy can provide additional information that may not be available through conventional visual skin assessment.

Magnified images allow practitioners to examine visible hair characteristics, distribution, variations in thickness and the skin surface.

Standardised images can also support documentation of changes between appointments.

In advanced systems, images may be transferred to software for analysis of selected features.

Potential applications include automated counting of visible hairs, hair thickness estimation, image comparison and identification of areas requiring further observation.

Accuracy depends on image quality, illumination, magnification and algorithm validation.

The presence of a dermoscope does not itself indicate artificial intelligence.

Dermoscopy does not replace medical dermatological assessment either. Suspicious skin lesions require appropriate medical evaluation.

An example of integrating an additional optical instrument into a hair removal platform is LUMOS, which can be equipped with a dermoscope in selected configurations.

### Does every intelligent laser use AI?

From an engineering perspective, several levels of automation should be distinguished.

#### Level 1. Factory treatment programmes

The operator selects a skin phototype, body area and hair type. The device proposes previously stored settings.

This is a preset-based system and does not necessarily involve artificial intelligence.

#### Level 2. Rule-based algorithms

Software processes information according to relationships established by the manufacturer.

For example, a pigmentation measurement may be associated with a predefined parameter range.

This can be more advanced than a basic preset but does not require machine learning.

#### Level 3. Feedback control

The device monitors a selected parameter and responds to changes.

Automatic cooling regulation using temperature measurements is one example.

This is control engineering and can operate without AI.

#### Level 4. Machine learning

The system uses a model developed from training data.

Such a model may analyse images, classify selected skin or hair characteristics and support decision-making.

Its value depends on data quality, validation and the conditions under which the system was evaluated.

The model does not necessarily learn during each treatment. It may use previously trained parameters.

![Levels of automation](https://ltsmarket.pl/assets/img/blog/ai-hair-removal/en/automation-levels.svg)

Levels of automation

### How might an intelligent operator support system work?

An advanced system may combine information from multiple sources.

During assessment, it may collect information about skin pigmentation, visible hair characteristics and the treatment area.

Software can then relate the measurements to the intended operating conditions of the device and present relevant information or recommendations to the practitioner.

During operation, the system may monitor selected technical parameters, including handpiece temperature or skin contact.

Abnormal conditions may trigger a warning or emission interlock if supported by the equipment architecture.

After treatment, stored information can assist with documentation.

Practitioner control remains essential. Software recommendations should not replace client assessment, knowledge of contraindications or compliance with manufacturer instructions.

![Operator support system](https://ltsmarket.pl/assets/img/blog/ai-hair-removal/en/intelligent-control-loop.svg)

Operator support system

### Emerging technology and future developments

In 2025, European patent application EP4537779A1 was published, describing a concept for selecting laser handpiece parameters through analysis of skin and hair characteristics.

The document describes the potential use of a hyperspectral camera, additional sensors and neural networks for classifying skin and hair characteristics and generating recommended settings [[6]](https://data.epo.org/publication-server/rest/v1.2/publication-dates/2025-04-16/patents/EP4537779NWA1/document.pdf).

Hyperspectral imaging captures image information across numerous spectral bands, providing more information than conventional RGB photography.

The patent application illustrates a possible direction for future technology.

However, it does not establish clinical effectiveness or demonstrate that the proposed features are commercially available in every modern device.

When evaluating innovative equipment, it is important to distinguish manufacturer claims, technical documentation, patent applications and clinical research.

### Electronic treatment records

Another practical area of development involves storing treatment information.

Records may include appointment dates, anatomical treatment areas, handpiece selection, device settings and practitioner notes.

Such documentation can support the assessment of subsequent appointments and continuity of care in clinics employing several practitioners.

Where photographs or identifiable client information are stored, appropriate data protection and compliance with applicable privacy requirements are necessary.

Maintaining treatment records is not artificial intelligence, but it can be a valuable feature of modern equipment.

### What should you consider when buying an AI-enabled laser?

Before purchasing equipment marketed as intelligent, practitioners should ask the manufacturer several questions:

1. Which parameters does the device actually measure?
2. Is pigmentation assessment quantitative or based on colour classification?
3. Where is the temperature sensor located?
4. Does the device monitor parameters during emission?
5. Does the software recommend settings or automatically modify them?
6. Which protective systems operate independently of the AI model?
7. Are validation results available?
8. Which skin phototypes and hair characteristics were evaluated?
9. How is client information stored and protected?
10. Can the device operate without an internet connection?
11. Are software updates and technical support available?

If a manufacturer cannot explain which data the system analyses, the AI label alone provides insufficient information about its capabilities.

### Will artificial intelligence replace practitioners?

The greatest current potential of intelligent systems lies in supporting practitioners.

Automation may reduce repetitive tasks, improve documentation and provide additional information during skin assessment.

It does not replace client interviews, professional assessment, knowledge of contraindications or the ability to respond to adverse reactions.

Even advanced algorithms require accurate input data and appropriate use of equipment.

The development of artificial intelligence does not eliminate the importance of practitioner experience. Instead, it may provide practitioners with more accurate and useful tools.

### Conclusion

The future of laser hair removal will probably involve not only improvements in laser sources but also improvements in the quality of information used during treatments.

Melanin measurements, spectrophotometry, dermoscopy, sensors and automatic control systems may become important elements of this development.

Their value should be assessed through actual functionality, measurement quality and validated capabilities rather than the presence of an AI label.

At LTS Market, we focus on technologies that have practical relevance to professional aesthetic equipment operation.

In the next article in this series, we will examine the possibilities of combining laser hair removal with other aesthetic technologies.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Does an AI-enabled laser automatically select every treatment parameter?

Not necessarily. Automation depends on the device architecture. Some systems provide only presets or recommendations.

#### Does skin phototype represent exact melanin content?

No. Phototype primarily describes skin responses to sunlight. Optical measurements can provide additional pigmentation information.

#### Does intelligent cooling require artificial intelligence?

No. Automatic temperature regulation can use conventional feedback control.

#### Does a dermoscope indicate the presence of AI?

No. A dermoscope is an optical instrument. AI-based image analysis requires additional software.

#### Does artificial intelligence eliminate the risk of complications?

No. Intelligent systems may support practitioners but cannot eliminate every risk or replace appropriate client assessment.

### Ultrasonic cavitation and body contouring

Radiofrequency, or RF, uses energy that heats tissue. With suitable devices, it may improve skin appearance and firmness. This article refers to non-invasive RF applied at the skin surface, rather than RF microneedling.

The technologies address different aesthetic goals: local contours and skin appearance. Having both in one device can simplify the organisation of body treatment services and reduce the need to purchase separate machines.

## Dermoscopy: An Additional Tool for Laser Hair Removal Professionals

HTML source: [Dermoscopy: An Additional Tool for Laser Hair Removal Professionals](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/blog/dermatoscope-laser-hair-removal/)

Language: English

Other languages: [Polski](https://ltsmarket.pl/blog/dermatoskop-w-epilacji-laserowej/), [Русский](https://ltsmarket.pl/ru/blog/dermatoskop-v-lazernoy-epilyatsii/)

> Discover how dermoscopy supports hair and skin assessment, treatment documentation and professional consultations in laser hair removal.

LTS Market Blog

20.11.2026 · LTS Market

**Professional laser hair removal is about more than laser power, wavelengths and treatment settings. It also requires careful observation of the skin, an understanding of hair characteristics and a reliable way to monitor visible changes throughout a treatment course. A dermatoscope can provide valuable support in all three areas.**

### What can a dermatoscope reveal that the naked eye cannot?

Before a laser hair removal session, practitioners assess skin characteristics, hair colour, thickness, distribution and any visible concerns in the treatment area.

However, the naked eye cannot reveal every detail.

A dermatoscope is an optical instrument that uses magnification and specialised illumination to provide a closer view of the skin and hair.

It allows practitioners to examine visible hair shafts, differences in hair thickness, follicular openings and superficial skin structures in greater detail.

The dermoscopic examination of hair is also known as trichoscopy.

This non-invasive technique is widely used in dermatology, particularly in the evaluation of hair and scalp conditions. Some of its observational benefits are also relevant to professional laser hair removal.

![Lumos — Dermatoscope front view](https://ltsmarket.pl/assets/img/lumos/lumos-dermatoscope-front-1024.webp)

### Why does hair thickness matter?

Hair is not uniform, even within a single treatment area.

Thick, dark terminal hairs may grow alongside much finer and lighter hairs. Their response to laser treatment may differ considerably.

Laser hair removal relies on the absorption of light energy by melanin associated with the hair follicle.

For this reason, hair pigmentation and characteristics are important considerations when evaluating treatment suitability and expectations.

Magnified observation can help practitioners distinguish between different visible hair types.

However, a dermatoscope does not automatically measure melanin concentration, determine follicle depth or calculate safe laser settings.

Instead, it provides additional visual information that complements the consultation, skin phototype assessment and the equipment manufacturer's instructions.

### Monitoring treatment progress with greater detail

One of the challenges in laser hair removal is documenting progress objectively.

Clients often describe their results in general terms: less hair, slower regrowth or finer hair after several sessions.

These observations are useful, but they can be subjective.

Dermoscopy provides another way to examine visible changes.

A study published in 2023 compared handheld dermoscopy with conventional digital photography for hair counting in 73 women undergoing alexandrite laser hair removal.

The researchers found that the dermatoscope detected significantly more hairs than the digital camera, including fine hairs that were more difficult to capture through conventional photography.

This suggests that dermoscopy can be a useful tool when evaluating visible hair changes after laser treatment.

It does not mean that a dermatoscope automatically calculates treatment effectiveness.

Meaningful comparisons still require consistent imaging conditions, including the same treatment area, similar magnification and lighting, and appropriate timing in relation to shaving and previous sessions.

When these conditions are considered, magnified images may provide useful supporting documentation throughout a treatment course.

### Skin observation is just as important as hair observation

Laser hair removal professionals work with both hair and skin.

A dermatoscope allows closer examination of the skin surface, follicular openings and certain visible pigmentation or inflammatory changes.

This can support a more careful pre-treatment assessment.

If a practitioner notices an unusual pigmented lesion, a suspicious mole, significant inflammation or another concerning skin change, treatment of the affected area should be postponed pending appropriate medical assessment.

Dermoscopy does not authorise a beauty practitioner to diagnose skin cancer or other medical conditions without the required professional qualifications.

Its value in this setting is observational: it may help practitioners recognise when further medical evaluation is necessary.

### A better way to communicate with clients

Clients often want to understand why hair responds differently across treatment areas, why multiple sessions are needed and why some fine hairs remain.

Magnified images can make these discussions easier.

Rather than relying entirely on verbal explanations, practitioners can show visible differences in hair thickness and distribution.

This creates an opportunity to explain realistic treatment expectations and the biological variability of hair growth.

The objective is not to promise faster or guaranteed results.

It is to provide a clearer, more transparent consultation supported by direct observation.

### Why does software integration matter?

A dermatoscope provides magnification, but the way its images are displayed and managed can influence its usefulness in daily practice.

A digital dermatoscope connected to suitable software may allow practitioners to view images on a screen and discuss them with clients.

Depending on the actual capabilities of the system, software may also support image capture, documentation or comparison between visits.

These functions should always be verified against the manufacturer's technical documentation rather than assumed.

**[LUMOS](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/new/lumos/) is an example of a laser hair removal system that includes a dermatoscope and integrated software for using this tool within the device's operating environment.**

Such integration can make magnified observation a convenient part of the professional consultation process.

![Lumos — Dermatoscope side view](https://ltsmarket.pl/assets/img/lumos/lumos-dermatoscope-side-1024.webp)

### How might a practitioner use dermoscopy in everyday work?

Consider a client attending an initial laser hair removal consultation.

The practitioner reviews the client's history, evaluates skin phototype, examines the treatment area and checks for relevant contraindications.

A dermatoscope is then used to observe selected areas in greater detail.

The practitioner can examine visible differences in hair thickness and distribution, along with superficial skin characteristics.

If the equipment supports image storage and the client has provided appropriate consent, initial images may be retained for future comparison.

At subsequent appointments, the same area can be examined again under comparable conditions.

The resulting observations can help explain visible changes throughout the course.

If concerning skin findings are identified, the practitioner should refer the client for appropriate medical evaluation.

In this workflow, dermoscopy supports professional observation and documentation rather than replacing clinical judgement.

### Should your next laser include a dermatoscope?

When choosing a laser hair removal system, professionals naturally focus on wavelengths, power, cooling performance, handpiece ergonomics, reliability and technical support.

These remain essential purchasing considerations.

However, it is also worth evaluating how well the equipment supports the practitioner's broader workflow.

A dermatoscope does not increase laser power, guarantee better hair removal results or replace medical diagnostic equipment.

What it offers is a closer view of the skin and hair, potentially more informative documentation and a useful visual aid during client consultations.

For a professional clinic, these benefits can make the dermatoscope a worthwhile addition to the treatment environment.

**When investing in your next laser hair removal system, consider not only how the device performs the treatment, but also how it helps you understand and observe the skin and hair you work with.**

#### Scientific references

1. *Handheld dermatoscope versus digital camera for hair counts in laser facial hair removal.* 2023. PMID: 37381826.
2. *Trichoscopic changes in hair during treatment of hirsutism with 1064-nm neodymium:yttrium-aluminum-garnet laser.* 2015. PMID: 26223429.
3. *The dermatoscope in the hair clinic: Trichoscopy of scarring and nonscarring alopecia.* Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, 2023. PMID: 37591567.
4. *Role of Dermoscopy in Laser Therapy.* 2023. PMCID: PMC10506824.

## What Really Makes a Good Diode Laser? Power, ICE Flow Cooling and FAC Optics Explained

HTML source: [What Really Makes a Good Diode Laser? Power, ICE Flow Cooling and FAC Optics Explained](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/blog/diode-laser-power-ice-flow-fac/)

Language: English

Other languages: [Polski](https://ltsmarket.pl/blog/moc-lasera-ice-flow-fac/), [Русский](https://ltsmarket.pl/ru/blog/moshchnost-lazera-ice-flow-fac/)

> Discover why 2000–4000 W is only part of the story. A practical explanation of ICE Flow cooling, pulse settings and FAC laser optics.

LTS Market Blog

19.11.2026 · LTS Market

### A good laser is more than a wattage figure

When beauty professionals compare diode laser systems, power is often one of the first specifications they consider.

A handpiece rated at 2000 W, 3000 W or 4000 W may sound impressive. However, the number alone tells us surprisingly little about how a device performs during treatment.

What matters is how accurately the system delivers optical energy, how consistently it maintains the selected settings and how effectively it manages heat.

A modern diode laser combines several closely connected technologies.

The laser diodes generate light. Optical components guide that light towards the treatment area. Electronics control the pulses. Cooling systems manage temperature.

To understand the quality of a laser, we need to look at all these systems together.

Using Lumos as an example, let us examine three important technologies.

### 1. ICE Flow. Understanding laser cooling

Laser hair removal works by delivering light energy that is absorbed by melanin.

Part of this energy is converted into heat, which can affect structures associated with the hair follicle.

This process is based on selective photothermolysis.

However, melanin is also present in the epidermis. Excessive heating of the skin surface may therefore cause unwanted thermal effects.

Cooling helps manage this risk.

#### What exactly is ICE Flow?

ICE Flow is the name used for the cooling system associated with Lumos.

It should not be confused with a universal technical standard.

Modern laser cooling systems may incorporate circulating coolant, heat exchangers, temperature sensors, thermoelectric components and cooled contact surfaces.

The precise internal configuration of ICE Flow must be verified against the manufacturer's technical documentation.

Its essential purpose is temperature management during operation.

#### Why does temperature stability matter?

A cold treatment window does not automatically mean that a cooling system performs well during prolonged use.

Consider two laser handpieces.

Both feel cold before treatment begins.

The first maintains a stable temperature during repeated pulses.

The second gradually becomes warmer because its cooling system cannot remove heat quickly enough.

The difference becomes apparent under sustained operating conditions.

This is why professionals should consider cooling capacity and thermal stability rather than focusing only on the lowest advertised contact temperature.

#### Does better cooling make higher energy automatically safe?

No.

Epidermal cooling can improve treatment tolerance and reduce certain thermal risks.

However, safe parameter selection still depends on skin phototype, tanning, hair characteristics, wavelength, pulse duration and device design.

Cooling supports safe operation. It does not replace professional assessment or appropriate treatment protocols.

### 2. Why does a 2000–4000 W power range matter in 2026 and 2027?

Lumos is offered in configurations with a declared handpiece power range of 2000 to 4000 W.

Its published specifications include pulse energy from 10 to 240 J, repetition rates from 1 to 30 Hz and pulse durations starting at 5 ms.

These figures describe a potentially flexible operating range.

However, understanding the units is essential.

#### Watts, joules and fluence

Watts measure power, or the rate at which energy is transferred.

Joules measure energy.

Fluence describes the energy delivered per unit area and is commonly expressed in J/cm².

Two devices with the same advertised wattage may therefore deliver very different treatment characteristics.

Spot size, optical output, pulse duration, wavelength and beam distribution all matter.

It is also important to establish what a manufacturer means by handpiece power.

A specification may refer to optical output, peak power, electrical input or a combined nominal rating of laser emitters.

These values are not interchangeable.

#### What is power headroom?

Power headroom means having additional available capacity beyond what is required for a particular operating condition.

In principle, this can provide greater flexibility when generating pulses and maintaining selected output levels.

However, a larger power reserve is only useful when the optical, electronic and cooling systems can support it.

A powerful laser that cannot maintain its operating temperature may have to limit output during demanding treatment conditions.

The objective is not to operate at maximum power all the time.

The objective is to deliver the required energy accurately and consistently.

#### Why are adjustable parameters so important?

No single treatment setting is appropriate for every client.

Skin phototype, hair thickness, pigmentation, treatment area and individual tissue response all influence parameter selection.

Adjustable pulse energy, pulse duration and repetition rate provide flexibility within the device's approved operating protocols.

A shorter pulse delivers its energy over a shorter period.

A longer pulse spreads energy delivery over more time.

The clinical implications depend on the complete treatment configuration, not on pulse duration alone.

#### Does 30 Hz guarantee faster treatment?

Not necessarily.

A repetition rate of 30 Hz means that the system can generate 30 pulses per second in a supported operating mode.

It does not tell us how much energy is available at that rate.

For example, delivering 240 J at 30 Hz would require an average optical output of 7200 W if both maximum values were available simultaneously.

This illustrates why published maximum specifications must be interpreted carefully.

Maximum pulse energy and maximum repetition rate may refer to different operating conditions.

Professionals should request the actual combinations of settings supported by the device.

#### What matters most in 2026 and 2027?

Beauty clinics increasingly value consistent performance, flexible protocols, reliable operation and access to technical support.

A wide adjustment range and sufficient power capacity can help meet these expectations.

However, there is no universal scientific rule stating that a modern hair removal laser must deliver 4000 W.

Measured performance and appropriate treatment parameters remain more important than the largest number in a brochure.

### 3. FAC. How optical engineering controls laser light

FAC stands for Fast Axis Collimation.

It is an optical technique used to control the divergence of light emitted by laser diodes.

#### Why does diode laser light need optical correction?

A laser diode does not emit a perfectly parallel beam.

Light spreads as it leaves the emitting region.

This divergence is generally different along two perpendicular axes.

The direction with greater divergence is known as the fast axis.

Without optical correction, efficiently collecting and transporting the emitted light becomes more difficult.

#### How does FAC work?

A specially designed optical element, often a small cylindrical microlens, is positioned close to the laser emitter.

Its purpose is to reduce divergence along the fast axis.

This process is called collimation.

By controlling the direction of the emitted light, the optical system can guide it more effectively through subsequent components.

FAC does not generate additional laser energy.

It helps manage the energy that the diodes have already produced.

#### Why is FAC important in high power diode systems?

High power diode modules may contain multiple emitters.

Each emitter produces light that must be collected and guided through the optical system.

Poor optical alignment or unsuitable beam geometry can reduce the amount of usable light transmitted through the system.

FAC can improve optical collection and facilitate further beam shaping.

It is therefore an important part of the engineering behind many high power diode laser assemblies.

#### Does FAC guarantee better hair removal results?

No.

FAC is an optical engineering technique, not a clinical outcome guarantee.

Uniform energy distribution at the treatment window depends on the entire optical design.

Other lenses, beam shaping components, homogenisation optics and the treatment window also influence the final beam profile.

FAC should not be confused with a complete beam homogenisation system.

Actual optical measurements are needed to evaluate energy distribution and transmission efficiency.

### 4. Why do cooling, power and optics belong together?

These three technologies perform different functions, but their performance is interconnected.

A powerful laser source places greater demands on thermal management.

The optical system determines how effectively emitted light is transmitted towards the treatment window.

Electronics regulate pulse generation and output settings.

Cooling helps maintain suitable operating temperatures and contributes to epidermal protection.

The quality of a diode laser depends on how successfully these components work together.

This is why comparing devices solely by advertised handpiece wattage is insufficient.

### 5. Lumos as an example of modern diode laser engineering

Lumos combines several features associated with contemporary diode laser design.

These include declared 2000–4000 W handpiece configurations, a broad parameter range, ICE Flow cooling and FAC optical technology.

Together, they offer a useful starting point for evaluating the device.

However, technical specifications should always be considered alongside documentation, measured optical performance, cooling stability and serviceability.

At LTS Market, we believe that technical support is an important part of choosing professional equipment.

Customers purchasing equipment through LTS Market also receive service support from [Laser Tech Service](https://lasertechservice.pl/).

### Conclusion

A professional diode laser should not be judged by wattage alone.

Power capacity matters when it supports stable and controlled energy delivery.

A broad parameter range provides flexibility.

ICE Flow addresses temperature management, while FAC helps control laser beam divergence.

Each technology contributes to a different part of the system.

Understanding how they work together makes it easier to evaluate equipment and ask the right questions before purchasing.

- [Contact cooling of the skin](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10232811/)

- [Micro-optics assembly for fast axis collimation by means of convolutional neural network](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34615104/)

## How to Buy a Used Hair Removal Laser Without Getting Scammed: Shot Counters, Counterfeits and Hidden Faults

HTML source: [How to Buy a Used Hair Removal Laser Without Getting Scammed: Shot Counters, Counterfeits and Hidden Faults](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/blog/how-to-buy-a-used-hair-removal-laser-safely/)

Language: English

Other languages: [Polski](https://ltsmarket.pl/blog/jak-kupic-uzywany-laser-do-depilacji-bez-ryzyka/), [Русский](https://ltsmarket.pl/ru/blog/kak-kupit-bu-lazer-dlya-epilyatsii-bez-riska/)

> Learn how to check a used hair removal laser before buying. Shot counters, counterfeit devices, hidden faults, professional inspection and warranty.

LTS Market Blog

26.11.2026 · LTS Market

Buying a used hair removal laser does not require you to be an engineer, understand electronics or know how a laser handpiece is built. One of the most reliable ways to reduce the risk of a bad purchase is to have the equipment assessed by specialists who repair and maintain aesthetic lasers before you hand over your money. However, even when a seller demonstrates a low shot count, original documentation and a functioning device, there are important details every salon owner should understand.

### Why buying a used laser is similar to buying a used car

Imagine two cars manufactured in the same year. One has covered 70,000 kilometres, while the other has covered 150,000. Which would you choose?

At first glance, the answer seems obvious. But what if the first car has undergone major repairs, received irregular maintenance and had its mileage altered? Meanwhile, the second has a complete service history and has been maintained regularly.

The situation with aesthetic equipment is remarkably similar.

An attractive appearance, a low shot count and convincing assurances from the seller do not necessarily mean that a laser is in good technical condition or has a long remaining service life.

The most important components are located inside the device. Their condition cannot be assessed from photographs in an online listing.

### Can you trust a laser shot counter?

The number of pulses is one of the first parameters buyers consider when purchasing used equipment.

Understandably, buyers want to know how intensively a laser has been used and how long it might continue operating.

However, shot counters have limitations.

Depending on the design of the equipment, pulse count information may be stored in the control system, handpiece electronics or other components. During repairs or replacement of electronic boards or handpieces, the displayed count may change or be reset.

Not every counter reset indicates fraud. Sometimes it is a legitimate consequence of a repair. The problem arises when buyers are not informed about such interventions or are deliberately misled about the equipment's history.

Even if the shot counter displays an accurate number, another question remains: under what conditions was the laser operated?

Research into semiconductor laser degradation indicates that service life is influenced by factors including:

- laser diode temperature;

- operating electrical current;

- heat dissipation efficiency;

- optical output power;

- electrical overload;

- moisture exposure and component damage.

Two identical laser devices with the same shot count may be in completely different technical conditions.

A shot counter should therefore be treated as an additional source of information rather than a guarantee of remaining service life.

### The laser works, but does it deliver the required power?

The seller switches on the device. The display works, the cooling system starts and the handpiece generates pulses. Everything appears to be functioning correctly.

But do the actual laser emission parameters correspond to the values displayed on the screen?

A laser may generate pulses while delivering reduced or unstable output. Possible causes include diode module degradation, damaged optics, power supply problems or insufficient cooling.

Without suitable measurement equipment, these issues can be difficult to identify.

During a professional inspection, a specialist uses measuring instruments selected according to the laser type, wavelength and emission characteristics. The results are compared with the technical documentation for the specific model.

Output stability during operation is also important.

A device that performs successfully during a short demonstration may begin overheating or become unstable under prolonged operating conditions.

For a salon, this can mean interrupted treatments, dissatisfied clients and temporary business downtime.

### Counterfeit lasers: when a well-known brand exists only on the casing

Counterfeiting is not limited to car parts, clothing and consumer electronics. Copies of well-known brands also exist in the professional aesthetic equipment market.

Counterfeit aesthetic devices have been discussed in scientific journals including Lasers in Surgery and Medicine, Aesthetic Surgery Journal and the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology.

A convincing imitation may have a similar casing, user interface, handpiece and logo. This does not mean that it contains the same components, protective systems or radiation sources.

It is important to distinguish counterfeit equipment from affordable devices manufactured by other companies. A less familiar or budget-oriented brand is not necessarily inferior. The problem arises when one device is falsely represented as another or misleading information is provided about its origin.

Before purchasing a branded laser, consider checking:

- the device serial number;

- handpiece serial numbers, where applicable;

- the manufacturer's identification plate;

- whether the documentation matches the specific model;

- the equipment's origin;

- whether authenticity can be confirmed by the manufacturer.

If a seller cannot explain where the equipment came from, it is advisable not to rush into the purchase.

### Hidden faults that cannot be seen in photographs

Preparing equipment for resale may involve cleaning the casing, replacing external parts and correcting cosmetic damage.

This is normal practice, but the appearance of a device does not reveal the condition of its internal components.

A professional technical inspection may identify problems such as:

- reduced laser module output;

- evidence of internal coolant leaks;

- damaged optical components;

- insufficient coolant circulation;

- faulty fans or pumps;

- damaged handpiece cables;

- unstable power supply operation;

- consequences of improper repairs;

- faulty temperature monitoring systems.

A previous repair does not automatically make a device a poor choice.

A professionally repaired laser with documented component replacements and technical test results may be a better investment than equipment with an unknown operating history.

The important question is not whether the laser has been repaired, but what was repaired, who performed the work and what results were obtained afterwards.

### Is CE marking enough to ensure a safe purchase?

When purchasing aesthetic equipment in Poland, European conformity requirements must be considered.

Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2346 establishes common specifications for certain categories of products without an intended medical purpose, including laser and IPL equipment used for hair removal and other skin treatments.

For professional equipment covered by the relevant provisions, regular output monitoring is required, including measurement of light energy density at least annually in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.

However, CE marking does not confirm the current technical condition of a used device.

Equipment may have complied with applicable requirements when it was placed on the market but subsequently suffered damage, improper repairs or modifications.

Documentation verification and technical inspection therefore complement each other.

### How much does a cheap laser really cost?

Consider a hypothetical example.

A salon owner finds a used diode laser for PLN 25,000. Another device with similar specifications costs PLN 30,000 but has a documented service history, has undergone technical inspection and is sold with a warranty.

Initially, the first option appears more attractive.

Suppose that after purchasing the cheaper device, the laser handpiece and cooling system require repairs, followed by another diagnostic inspection.

| Expenses | Laser without prior inspection | Inspected laser |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purchase price | PLN 25,000 | PLN 30,000 |
| Handpiece repair | PLN 6,000 | PLN 0 |
| Cooling system repair | PLN 1,500 | PLN 0 |
| Diagnostics | PLN 600 | Included |
| Total expenses | PLN 33,100 | PLN 30,000 |

These figures are provided solely to illustrate a possible scenario and do not constitute a repair quotation for any specific device.

The example does not include losses associated with cancelled treatments, salon downtime or rescheduling client appointments.

Sometimes the most economical equipment is not the cheapest option, but the one that allows your business to operate reliably after purchase.

### What should you check before buying a used laser?

| Inspection item | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Serial numbers | Equipment identification |
| Documentation and origin | Authenticity and conformity verification |
| Shot counter | Assessment of available operating history |
| Service history | Information about repairs and maintenance |
| Laser module | Assessment of the radiation source |
| Output parameters | Verification of actual performance |
| Cooling system | Thermal stability |
| Handpiece and optics | Identification of damage and wear |
| Safety systems | Verification of protective functions |
| Spare parts availability | Future repair options |
| Warranty terms | Buyer protection after purchase |

Salon owners without technical training are not expected to perform all these checks themselves. Professional laser service specialists can assist with the assessment.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Can a shot counter determine the remaining service life of a laser?

No. A shot counter helps assess operating history but does not account for every factor contributing to wear. Technical diagnostics are required to assess the current condition. Even a professional inspection cannot guarantee an exact number of future pulses.

#### Can an altered laser shot counter be detected?

In some cases, discrepancies can be identified by reviewing service records, available system data and component replacement history. Recovering the actual historical shot count is not always possible.

#### Is it worth buying a repaired laser?

Yes, provided that repairs were performed professionally, the repair history is documented, and output parameters and safety systems have been checked.

#### Can a laser advertised on OLX be inspected before purchase?

Yes. With the seller's consent, a professional technical assessment can be arranged before making a purchase decision.

#### What warranty does LTS Market provide for used equipment?

Used equipment sold by LTS Market comes with a six-month commercial warranty subject to the published warranty terms.

### Buy equipment for your business, not for the repair workshop

A laser should generate revenue for your salon rather than create unexpected expenses during the first months of operation.

Used equipment can be an excellent option for opening a new salon or expanding an existing treatment portfolio. The important thing is understanding exactly what you are buying.

You do not have to reject an attractive offer because you are afraid of making the wrong decision. Arranging a professional inspection before purchasing can help reduce that risk.

## Laser hair removal as a business: why plan your salon opening for autumn?

HTML source: [Laser hair removal as a business: why plan your salon opening for autumn?](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/blog/laser-hair-removal-business/)

Language: English

Other languages: [Polski](https://ltsmarket.pl/blog/depilacja-laserowa-jako-biznes/), [Русский](https://ltsmarket.pl/ru/blog/lazernaya-epilyaciya-kak-biznes/)

> Planning a laser hair removal salon in Poland? Prepare an autumn launch, compare new and pre-owned equipment, and explore leasing and technical support.

LTS Market Blog

Autumn can be a quiet starting point: time to prepare your treatment room, learn how to use your equipment and welcome your first clients. If you are planning a laser hair removal business in Poland, start with a practical plan before choosing a particular laser.

### Can laser hair removal be a viable business?

Clients want convenience and a service they can understand. For a salon, that means clear consultations, well-organised appointments and honest communication. Avoid promising the same outcome to everyone or results after a single visit.

Buying a device does not establish profitability. Calculate rent, staffing, consumables, marketing, financing and a maintenance reserve. Compare these costs with realistic appointment numbers and the margin after expenses. Include a cautious scenario instead of assuming a full diary from the first month.

### Why consider an autumn launch?

After the holidays, many clients return to regular work and family routines. This creates an opportunity to discuss ongoing appointments without relying on a seasonal discount. Owners can use the preparation period for training, testing booking systems and creating clear client information.

The season does not determine whether a person is suitable for treatment. Questions about tanning, preparation and contraindications belong in an individual consultation based on the device instructions and a qualified assessment. Do not promise to complete the process by a particular date.

### What do you need to open a salon?

Premises, equipment, skills and organisation must work together. Plan the treatment area, hygiene, consultation records, data protection and booking process. Check the premises and the installation requirements of your chosen model before signing a lease.

Prepare a first-consultation process, rescheduling terms and a way to provide aftercare instructions. Verify the requirements for your particular business and equipment with the appropriate specialists before opening. Purchasing a laser does not replace professional preparation.

### How should you choose a hair removal laser?

A diode laser should suit your intended services, budget and team. Compare the model’s intended use, documentation, handpiece ergonomics, cooling, installation needs and access to technical support. A headline specification alone cannot tell you what daily operation will be like.

Ask for a demonstration and an explanation of the controls. Confirm what the price, training and warranty cover, along with potential ongoing costs. Explore [new beauty equipment at LTS Market](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/nowe.html) and ask about a model suited to your planned treatments.

### New or pre-owned equipment?

Compare specific offers rather than treating all new or used devices as equivalent. For a pre-owned laser, ask about the production year, service history, handpiece condition, checks performed, included accessories and warranty terms.

Browse [pre-owned equipment at LTS Market](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/uzywane.html). Confirm hair removal laser availability and the condition of the individual unit. A lower purchase price is useful only when you also understand the ongoing costs.

### Buying outright or leasing a cosmetic laser?

Paying outright reduces future instalments but leaves less cash for launching the business. Financing can spread the expense, while introducing costs and commitments that need careful comparison: the initial payment, instalments, buyout and contract terms.

Visit the [beauty equipment leasing page](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/leasing.html) to discuss financing with LTS Market. Availability and terms require individual confirmation. Your budget should also accommodate quieter months.

### Why does technical service matter?

Downtime affects more than repair costs: it can mean rescheduled appointments and extra client communication. Before purchasing, ask about maintenance, spare parts, fault reporting and equipment transport arrangements.

Explore [beauty equipment servicing at Laser Tech Service](https://lasertechservice.pl/uslugi/). Confirm support for your particular model and the available service scope directly with the team. Do not build your business plan around an unconfirmed repair turnaround.

### How can you prepare for your first clients?

Show a clean treatment room, explain the consultation and describe how you prepare for appointments. Use plain language and obtain permission before publishing material involving clients. You do not need promises of a perfect result to explain the value of a professional service.

Build relationships with nearby salons, keep your business details clear and make booking straightforward. Address interested clients of all genders. Discuss follow-up appointments according to individual plans, without pressure or unsupported promises.

### Common mistakes when opening a salon

Choosing solely on price, keeping no financial reserve and postponing training can make the launch harder. So can a disorganised diary or advertising that promises more than you can justify.

Do not accept every booking at any cost. Clear suitability checks, the ability to decline a treatment and respectful communication belong in professional client care. Start with a consistent process you can maintain every day.

### Turn the idea into a practical plan

Write down your intended services, equipment budget and monthly expenses. Compare available models, purchase terms and support, then plan team preparation and a realistic opening schedule.

[Contact LTS Market](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/kontakt.html) with your plans for a salon in Poland. Include your budget and whether you are considering new equipment, a pre-owned device or leasing. This provides a useful starting point for discussing available options.

## Combined aesthetic technologies: laser hair removal, photorejuvenation and personalised treatment programmes

HTML source: [Combined aesthetic technologies: laser hair removal, photorejuvenation and personalised treatment programmes](https://ltsmarket.pl/en/blog/laser-hair-removal-ipl-bbl-combined-treatments/)

Language: English

Other languages: [Polski](https://ltsmarket.pl/blog/epilacja-laserowa-ipl-bbl-zabiegi-laczone/), [Русский](https://ltsmarket.pl/ru/blog/lazernaya-epilyatsiya-ipl-bbl-kombinirovannye-protsedury/)

> Explore the differences between laser hair removal, IPL, BBL, fractional lasers and RF, and their roles in combined aesthetic treatment programmes.

LTS Market Blog

25.11.2026 · LTS Market

*The future of laser hair removal: technology, effectiveness and safety. Part 3.*

For many years, aesthetic clinics specialised in individual treatment categories. Some focused on unwanted hair reduction, while others concentrated on skin appearance, pigmentation or rejuvenation procedures.

Developments in energy-based aesthetic equipment are gradually changing this model. More clinics are using several technologies to address different client needs.

A client receiving laser hair removal may also be interested in improving skin tone, reducing the appearance of visible vessels, improving skin texture or addressing selected scars.

However, this does not mean that all these concerns can be addressed with one laser or during a single appointment.

Understanding the mechanisms, indications and limitations of different technologies is essential when developing combined treatment programmes.

### Why do different technologies affect the skin differently?

One of the most important concepts in laser technology is the chromophore.

A chromophore is a component of tissue capable of absorbing light within particular wavelength ranges.

Three chromophores are especially relevant in aesthetic treatments and dermatology:

- Melanin, which contributes to skin and hair pigmentation.

- Haemoglobin, which is present in blood.

- Water, which is a major component of biological tissues.

Each has different optical absorption characteristics.

By selecting appropriate wavelengths and pulse parameters, energy can be directed towards particular tissue structures.

This principle forms the basis of selective photothermolysis, described by Anderson and Parrish in 1983.

However, not every aesthetic technology uses light. Radiofrequency systems rely on the interaction of high-frequency electrical energy with tissue and the resulting thermal effects.

Equipment intended for hair reduction, photorejuvenation, vascular treatments and skin remodelling is therefore not automatically interchangeable.

### Laser hair removal: targeting hair follicle structures

In laser hair removal, the primary chromophore is melanin within the hair.

Absorbed optical energy is converted into heat, affecting structures involved in hair growth.

Professional equipment includes:

- 755 nm alexandrite lasers.

- Diode lasers, commonly operating around 800–810 nm.

- 1064 nm Nd:YAG lasers.

- Multi-wavelength diode platforms.

Treatment effectiveness depends not only on wavelength but also on hair characteristics, skin pigmentation, hair growth phase, pulse parameters and cooling.

The primary objective is long-term hair reduction.

A laser designed for hair removal should not automatically be considered suitable for pigmentation treatments, vascular procedures or skin resurfacing.

Even where a particular wavelength is used for different applications, device architecture, pulse duration, energy delivery and intended use remain important.

### IPL: intense pulsed light

Intense pulsed light, or IPL, uses pulses of light covering a broad spectral range.

Unlike a typical laser, an IPL system does not emit one specific wavelength.

The light source is commonly a xenon flashlamp. Optical filters restrict the spectral range reaching the skin.

Depending on device architecture, filters and manufacturer-defined indications, IPL may be used for:

- Hair reduction.

- Selected pigmentation concerns.

- Superficial vascular concerns.

- Improving the appearance of photodamaged skin.

The versatility of IPL primarily comes from the ability to use different spectral ranges and pulse characteristics.

However, not every IPL device offers equivalent capabilities.

Filter quality, energy stability, pulse characteristics, cooling and technical documentation are all important.

### BBL: is it a separate type of laser?

BroadBand Light, or BBL, is the name of a broadband pulsed light technology developed by Sciton.

From a physical perspective, it belongs to the IPL family of technologies.

BBL is not a separate type of laser.

Specific BBL platforms may differ from other IPL devices in handpiece architecture, optical filters, pulse generation, cooling and energy control.

Depending on the platform and its indications, BBL may be used for pigmentation concerns, vascular concerns, signs of photodamage and hair reduction.

The term BBL should not be used as a generic name for every broadband pulsed light device.

When purchasing equipment, practitioners should evaluate the actual specifications and capabilities of the system rather than relying solely on its commercial name.

### Photorejuvenation and laser hair removal

Although both procedures can use optical energy, their objectives are different.

Hair removal primarily targets structures within the hair follicle.

IPL or BBL photorejuvenation may aim to improve skin appearance by addressing selected pigmentary and vascular concerns and features associated with photodamage.

Scientific reviews of IPL indicate that the technology can improve the appearance of skin affected by photoageing.

Outcomes depend on the type of concern, equipment, treatment parameters and individual skin characteristics.

Photorejuvenation should not be presented as a universal solution for every pigmentation concern.

Certain conditions, including melasma, require particular caution. Suspicious skin lesions should receive appropriate medical assessment before light-based treatment.

### Fractional lasers: controlled skin remodelling

Fractional lasers represent another category of aesthetic equipment.

Their mechanism involves creating microscopic treatment zones separated by areas that are not directly exposed to the laser beam.

This approach forms the basis of fractional photothermolysis, described in scientific literature in 2004.

Fractional technologies can be divided into ablative and non-ablative systems.

#### Ablative fractional lasers

Examples include:

- CO2 lasers operating at 10,600 nm.

- Er:YAG lasers operating at 2,940 nm.

Their primary chromophore is water.

Under appropriate conditions, laser energy removes microscopic areas of tissue and initiates a controlled healing response.

These technologies are used in procedures addressing selected scars, skin texture irregularities and signs of photoageing.

Ablative treatments may involve longer recovery periods and require appropriate client assessment and aftercare.

#### Non-ablative fractional lasers

Non-ablative technologies create controlled thermal treatment zones without conventional surface ablation.

Examples include certain systems operating around 1,540 or 1,550 nm.

Applications may include improving skin texture, reducing the appearance of selected scars and stimulating tissue remodelling.

Recovery periods may be shorter than those associated with ablative treatments, although this depends on treatment parameters and individual skin responses.

### Radiofrequency as a complement to light-based technologies

Radiofrequency, commonly abbreviated as RF, uses high-frequency electrical energy.

Thermal effects arise through the interaction of electrical current with tissue and depend on tissue electrical properties, electrode configuration and device parameters.

Unlike lasers and IPL, RF does not rely directly on selective light absorption by melanin or haemoglobin.

Aesthetic applications include:

- Monopolar radiofrequency.

- Bipolar radiofrequency.

- Multipolar systems.

- Radiofrequency microneedling.

These technologies differ in energy delivery, treatment depth and safety profile.

RF may form part of programmes intended to improve skin firmness and texture.

However, radiofrequency is not equivalent to laser hair removal or a universal replacement for fractional lasers.

Radiofrequency microneedling disrupts the skin barrier and requires particular attention to client assessment, hygiene and safety.

### Comparing the main technologies

| Technology | Mechanism or primary optical target | Typical application |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hair removal laser | Hair melanin | Long-term hair reduction |
| IPL | Melanin and haemoglobin, depending on filters | Selected pigmentation and vascular concerns, photorejuvenation and hair reduction |
| BBL | Broadband pulsed light | Applications depending on platform configuration |
| Fractional CO2 | Water | Ablative skin remodelling and selected scars |
| Fractional Er:YAG | Water | Ablative resurfacing |
| Non-ablative fractional laser | Tissue water | Controlled skin remodelling |
| RF | Interaction of electrical energy with tissue | Improving skin firmness and texture |

This table describes general mechanisms. Specific indications depend on the equipment, manufacturer documentation and individual client assessment.

### Can laser hair removal be combined with other treatments?

Different technologies can form part of an individual treatment programme.

However, a combined programme does not necessarily mean performing every procedure during one appointment.

For example, a client may receive a course of laser hair removal and attend a separate IPL appointment addressing a particular pigmentation concern.

Another client may proceed to treatments intended to improve skin texture after completing an appropriate stage of their hair removal programme.

Each procedure should have its own justification and be preceded by appropriate assessment.

When different technologies are used on the same anatomical area, important considerations include:

- Current skin condition.

- Response to previous treatments.

- Cumulative thermal exposure.

- Skin barrier integrity.

- Risk of pigmentation changes.

- Contraindications.

- Manufacturer recommendations.

There is no universal treatment interval suitable for every possible combination of technologies.

Scheduling should account for treatment type, intensity, recovery and individual skin characteristics.

Using more technologies does not automatically produce better outcomes.

### Paradoxical hair growth and the importance of assessment

One less obvious concern associated with light-based treatments is paradoxical hypertrichosis.

This is an unwanted increase in hair growth following laser or IPL treatment.

A meta-analysis published in 2021, covering 22 studies and 9,733 patients, estimated a pooled prevalence of approximately 3%.

The phenomenon was particularly associated with treatment of the face and neck. Reported prevalence outside these areas was substantially lower.

The authors also reported considerable heterogeneity between studies, meaning that this figure should not be interpreted as the precise individual risk associated with every client or device.

These findings highlight the importance of considering hair characteristics, treatment location and appropriate indications for optical energy exposure.

Additional skin areas should not be exposed to light-based treatment simply because the equipment offers that capability.

### One multifunctional device or several specialised platforms?

For aesthetic clinic owners, equipment selection also has an economic dimension.

A multifunctional platform may incorporate several handpiece types, enabling different procedures to be performed using one base unit.

Potential advantages include:

- Reduced space requirements.

- A shared user interface.

- Gradual expansion of treatment offerings.

- Potentially lower initial equipment costs.

However, limitations should also be considered.

Failure of a shared power supply, cooling system or controller may make several treatment functions unavailable simultaneously.

Specialised equipment allows individual treatment stations to operate independently.

This can be particularly useful in clinics where several practitioners perform different procedures at the same time.

Nevertheless, a specialised device is not necessarily more effective than a multifunctional platform. Performance depends on the architecture and specifications of the particular equipment.

### Evaluating the economic value of equipment

Equipment purchasing decisions should consider not only the purchase price but also the total cost of ownership.

Relevant expenses include consumables, handpieces, maintenance, repairs, practitioner training and potential downtime.

For multifunctional platforms, it is important to establish whether the advertised technologies are supported by appropriate documentation and whether spare parts are available.

Clinic owners should also identify which treatments correspond to genuine client demand.

Purchasing equipment with numerous functions may not be economically justified if most of those functions remain unused.

Equipment expansion should follow a clinic development strategy rather than the number of features listed in a manufacturer's brochure.

### What should you consider before purchasing equipment?

Before making a decision, establish:

- What is the intended use of each handpiece?

- Are the advertised functions supported by documentation?

- What are the actual energy delivery specifications?

- Can individual modules operate independently?

- Are spare parts available?

- What are the consumable costs?

- Is professional technical support available?

- What practitioner qualifications and training are required?

- Does the conformity documentation meet the requirements applicable to the equipment?

For aesthetic equipment using electromagnetic radiation, relevant European regulations should also be considered, including requirements applicable to products covered by Annex XVI of the Medical Device Regulation, where relevant.

### Conclusion

Developments in energy-based aesthetics involve more than increasing equipment power or adding new features.

The ability to select and use different technologies according to individual client needs and equipment capabilities is becoming increasingly important.

Laser hair removal, IPL, BBL, fractional lasers and radiofrequency have different mechanisms of action and can complement one another within individually planned treatment programmes.

Combining them requires knowledge, appropriate client assessment and adherence to safety principles.

At LTS Market, we focus not only on equipment functionality but also on technical condition, service availability and practical value in everyday aesthetic clinic operations.

In the next article in this series, we will examine the technologies influencing laser hair removal speed and comfort: power, treatment spot size, optics and cooling systems.
